A former freelance labour consultant complained that the company's director read and intervened in his work email correspondence on the company account without any notice to staff. The Garante found the company gave no information on email use or shared mailboxes, the monitoring was excessive, and the reciprocal processor appointments with its subsidiary were too generic to meet Article 28. It fined the company EUR 40,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The Article 6 charge was dropped.

A public employee complained, through his lawyer, that his unit commander had sent a police headquarters the full medical board report on his fitness for service, including diagnosis and medication, to support a weapons-licence check. The police then forwarded the full report to two other local police offices. The Garante found that the Ministry of the Interior had unlawfully communicated health data, in breach of Articles 19 and 20 of the Italian Privacy Code as it read before the GDPR, and ordered it to pay EUR 4,000. The processing took place before the GDPR applied, so the pre-2018 Code governed the case.

A complainant received a Mastercard credit card at her home address in February 2021 although she had never applied for it or had any contract with the bank Rewire EU B.V. She also said the bank did not answer her access request of April 2021. The Dutch authority, as lead supervisory authority, found that the bank had acted properly once it identified the account as fraudulent, and it found no proven breach of Articles 6(1) or 15 GDPR. The Garante adopted that draft decision under Article 60(8) GDPR, declared the complaint unfounded and archived it.

A user of the controller's encrypted email service complained that the free tier only let users export emails one at a time, while paying users could export in bulk. The Ombudsman found that the controller had not fulfilled the right to data portability under Article 20(1) and had not provided it free of charge as Article 12(5) requires. Because the bulk export tool was limited to paying users, the right was in practice available only for a fee. The Ombudsman issued a reprimand under Article 58(2)(b) and no fine is mentioned. The controller had by then made the tool available to free users.

The Finnish DPA found a city in Finland responsible for organising primary education infringing multiple GDPR provisions, as personal data of pupils were made visible to an unnecessarily wide group of people through MS Office 365 e-mail address book.

The Belgian DPA rejected several complaints against Meta following a data leakage, considering that it was bound by a previous Irish DPC's decision on that matter, even though the DPC decision focused on other GDPR provisions than the complaints.

A complaint said the council had a CCTV camera in an office that recorded staff and visitors, with no warning signs. The council said the camera was used to check subscription payments and that staff had signed consent forms. The Commissioner found no valid legal basis under Article 6, because employees could not give free consent to their employer, and found a breach of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6. No fine was imposed; the council was ordered to stop using the camera, remove or cover it, delete any recordings, and report back within two weeks.

The press release reports two investigations in the medical sector, both started by complaints from individuals. For the medical centre, the authority found that it sent a WhatsApp message to one person's phone containing the results of two medical tests belonging to two other people. It held that the centre had not applied adequate technical and organisational security measures, so the data was disclosed and accessed without authorisation. The centre was fined RON 4,918.50 (stated as EUR 1,000) and ordered to review its security measures and keep a register of personal data breaches. The second investigation, against Med Life S.A., is in the same release but is not part of this decision.

The CNIL fined a scooter rental company €125,000 for various privacy violations. Among the others, the collection of geo-location data every 30 second was not necessary for the purpose pursued by the controller.

A consultancy firm notified the AEPD of a confidentiality breach after a backpack containing an unencrypted USB drive was stolen. The drive held personal data relating to criminal offences and convictions. The AEPD rejected the firm's arguments that no breach had occurred, that it was not at fault, and that its security measures were adequate. It found that the firm stored the data on an unprotected removable device and did not follow the security measures it had put in place. It imposed two fines: EUR 90,000 for breaching Article 5(1)(f) GDPR and EUR 55,000 for breaching Article 32 GDPR, EUR 145,000 in total.

A data subject complained that his personal data was used to create a profile in a telecom operator's app, through a so-called 'e-signature' function, although he never signed the application. The operator's shop staff had not properly identified the person, and the complainant's objections sent on 17 and 23 February 2022 were filtered into spam and not acted on. The function was deactivated on 15 June 2022. The Commission found a breach of the purpose limitation and integrity/confidentiality principles and of Article 24, and imposed a fine of 2,000 BGN.

A press release from the Romanian DPA reports that, after an investigation finished in February 2023, the party Alianța pentru Unirea Românilor was fined RON 49,115 (about EUR 10,000). It collected personal data, including national ID numbers, through an online form, postal forms and special centres. This breached data minimisation and accountability. The same release also reports a separate EUR 4,000 fine against another party (Partidul Uniunea Salvați România) under Art. 32, which is not part of this decision.

A press release from the Romanian authority reports two sanctions; the one relevant here concerns the party Uniunea Salvați România. After the party notified a personal data breach, the authority found that a server hosting an application was hit by a phishing attack and that stored data (including political affiliation) was accessed without authorisation. The party had not implemented adequate technical and organisational measures such as encryption or pseudonymisation. It was fined 19,646 lei (about EUR 4,000) and ordered to bring processing into compliance by implementing appropriate measures based on a risk assessment.

The Spanish DPA closed sanctioning proceedings against Vodafone España after the company paid a proposed fine early. The December 2022 initial agreement proposed three fines totalling EUR 170,000 for alleged breaches of Articles 6 and 32 GDPR, linked to a fraudulent phone-number portability, an unauthorised change of the complainant's e-mail address and a duplicate invoice issued to a third party. Vodafone paid EUR 136,000, which is the 20% reduction applied, but did not admit liability. The resolution therefore terminated the procedure under Article 85 of the Spanish administrative procedure law, with no finding on the merits.

The Romanian data protection authority finished an investigation in February 2023 into Tinmar Energy SA. The investigation began after the company notified a personal data breach. Unauthorised persons had accessed the company's e-mail server and reached personal data such as names, e-mail addresses, personal numeric codes, phone numbers and home addresses. The authority found that the company had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security suited to the risk, and fined it RON 14,702.1, stated as the equivalent of EUR 3,000.

The Belgian DPA emphasizes that the controller is responsible for replying to data subject access requests, regardless of employee circumstances such as long-term sick leaves or simply forgetting about it.

The Romanian authority investigated Modaone SRL, which operates an online shop, after a data subject complained of receiving marketing emails despite having objected. The investigation found that the company did not provide complete information under Article 13 GDPR and imposed excessive conditions for exercising data subject rights, breaching Articles 12 and 13. The company was fined 9871 lei (stated as EUR 2000) and ordered to take corrective measures.

The DPA held that the disclosure of personal data of debtors in a public Facebook group was unlawful and ordered the controller to stop the processing. The administrator of the group cannot rely on any legitimate or public interest.

A complaint was made that the Austurmiðstöð unit of Reykjavík City sent, by email to an unauthorised recipient, a password-protected report containing a child's health data, with the password sent in a second email to the same address. The Icelandic DPA found the disclosure had no legal basis and was not lawful, and that the City did not ensure adequate security as required by Article 32 GDPR and section 27 of Act No. 90/2018. It noted the City reported the breach within 72 hours, informed the parents and asked the recipient to delete the emails. It found no need to issue specific orders to the City.

After an inspection by the Guardia di Finanza, the Garante fined a sole-trader fruit and vegetable shop EUR 3,000. The inspection found a working camera that filmed the shop floor, including employees, with no information sign and without the labour-authority authorisation required by Art. 4 of Law 300/1970. The Garante declared the processing unlawful under Article 5(1)(a), Article 13 GDPR and Article 114 of the Italian Privacy Code, and rejected the trader's claim that the camera was not working because the official report has full evidential value. The trader's later removal of the camera, documented to the Garante, was counted as mitigation, and the decision is ordered to be published on the Garante's website.

Seven employees complained to the Garante that Deca s.r.l. had not answered their requests for access to their badge attendance data, and also complained about video surveillance. The investigation, including a Guardia di finanza inspection, found no evidence of how the company had answered the access requests; its claim of hand delivery was undocumented and disputed. The video surveillance complaint was not substantiated. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR and fined the company EUR 1,600, ordering publication of the decision.

A former employee and financial adviser of Invest Banca asked for access to his personal data on 5 May 2021 and received no reply within the legal deadline. He complained to the Garante, and the bank answered in full only in September 2021, during the procedure, blaming technical problems, the extraordinary administration and remote working. Invest Banca had meanwhile merged into Banca Cambiano 1884, which took over liability. The Garante rejected the bank's justifications, found breaches of Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR and fined the bank EUR 10,000, ordering publication of the decision.

A data subject complained about an unsolicited marketing call for boiler maintenance from a small company, and about its evasive answer on where his data came from. The company had bought contact lists from a Spanish supplier not named in the decision, without checking that the people on them had consented or been informed, and it sent a 5,776-contact Excel file to the complainant. The Garante found breaches of the lawfulness, consent and information rules, of the access-request rules, and of the rules on unlawful disclosure to third parties. It imposed a EUR 3,000 fine, ordered deletion of the file, banned further use of the supplier's data, required procedures to be adopted if third-party contact data is used again, and ordered publication of the decision.

A former trainee complained that, after his internship ended in February 2020, the consortium kept his individual company email account active until 6 April 2020, accessed incoming messages from public-administration clients, and never gave him a privacy notice about this. The Garante found breaches of Article 5(1)(a) and (c), Article 12 and Article 13 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000. It archived the allegations under Article 5(1)(e) and under Article 12 read with Article 15.

Argon Medical Devices, a US company, suffered a cyber security incident in 2021 in which an HR executive's mailbox was accessed, exposing salary and benefits data of all its European employees, including one in Norway. Datatilsynet found Argon knew of the breach by at least 19 July 2021 but notified it only 67 calendar days later, well past the 72-hour deadline. Argon had treated the clock as starting only once it had a full picture of the incident. Datatilsynet fined Argon NOK 2,500,000 for infringing Article 33(1) GDPR. It stressed deterrence and rejected Argon's comparison with an earlier Telenor reprimand. Argon may appeal within three weeks.

After acknowledging that technical log generated by a security device installed in the data subject's house is personal data, the Spanish DPA fined a security company for failing to comply with an order to provide this information to the data subject and imposed a fine of €50,000.

An Austrian website using Facebook tracking tools was found in breach of Article 44 GDPR for the transfer of data to the US without any legal basis. The fact that the tools were deactivated after the complaint was considered irrelevant.

The Romanian DPA finished two investigations in February 2023 into Finopro IFN SA and Integral Collection SRL, both started after the controllers notified personal data breaches. Ransomware attacks caused unauthorised access to personal data and loss of its integrity and availability. The authority found that neither controller had put appropriate technical and organisational security measures in place, in breach of Art. 32(1)(b) and (c) and 32(2) GDPR. Finopro IFN SA was fined RON 11,023.42 (about EUR 2,250) and Integral Collection SRL RON 14,697.90 (about EUR 3,000).

The Romanian authority finished two investigations in February 2023, into Finopro IFN SA and Integral Collection SRL. Both had notified personal data breaches caused by ransomware attacks, which led to unauthorised access and loss of integrity and availability of personal data. The authority found that neither had implemented technical and organisational measures appropriate to the risk, in breach of Article 32(1)(b) and (c) and 32(2) GDPR. Integral Collection SRL was fined RON 14,697.90, stated to be equivalent to EUR 3,000. The press release covers both operators; only the Integral Collection part is used here.

A complainant sent access and copy requests under Article 15 GDPR to the controller on 7 September 2022 and sent a reminder on 10 October 2022, but received no reply. After an APD letter of 19 January 2023 told him to use a different contact address, he repeated the request that day and still had no answer by 26 February 2023. The Belgian APD's Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision, not a decision on the merits, finding that the controller may have breached Articles 15 and 12 GDPR. It ordered the controller to comply with the access request within 30 days, gave a warning to answer future data subject requests, and required it to report compliance to the APD. The controller may ask for a merits review within 30 days.

An employee of a Belgian care home complained that the home had published her first and last name in a notice and an open letter to staff, after she requested a formal psychosocial intervention about violence and harassment. The Litigation Chamber examined whether the publication had a legal basis under Article 6(1). It found that neither the legal obligation (6(1)(c)) nor the legitimate interest (6(1)(f)) applied, because naming her was not necessary to inform staff of the external adviser's findings. The chamber issued a prima facie decision: a warning that such publication could breach Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1) GDPR, and an order to comply with her erasure request. No fine was imposed.

This is a newsletter item, not the decision itself. The Garante fined the Bari local health authority EUR 50,000. Over six years its website section 'Parlano bene di noi' published praise letters and forms from hundreds of patients, containing identifying details and health information such as diagnoses and anamnesis. Some were 'redacted' only by hand with a black marker, which still left them readable and the authors identifiable. The Garante stressed that health data may not be disseminated and that manual marker or correction-fluid redaction is neither anonymisation nor pseudonymisation.

The Garante received several complaints about unsolicited promotional emails sent for various clients by a sole trader running an email marketing service from Croatia under a false trade name and a made-up personal name. The trader sent campaigns to addresses found online or randomly generated, without any consent, for over a year and to thousands of people. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1)(a) GDPR and Article 130 of the Code. It banned the processing, ordered deletion of the data, and fined the business EUR 5,000, with publication of the decision.

The Garante investigated Razmataz Live, which promoted cultural events for clients by using a third-party supplier to send promotional emails, as found in the earlier case against Colosseo S.r.l. that arose from two complaints. The company ignored the Garante's request for information. The Garante found that Razmataz acted de facto as a processor, did no checks on the supplier it chose, and could not show the complainant's consent. It declared the processing unlawful, ordered Razmataz to adopt procedures to verify documented consent if it uses third parties for promotion in future, and imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 plus publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA held that, under national law implementing Article 9 GDPR, the processing of health data for scientific purposes can be carried out without explicit consent when the collection entails a disproportionate effort or impairs the research purposes. In such cases, suitable safeguards to protect privacy and security of the data must be provided.

Following a report by a trade union about CCTV systems in H&M's Italian stores, the Garante carried out inspections in April-May 2022. It found that the company used video surveillance in several stores without completing the union agreement or labour inspectorate authorisation procedure required by Article 4 of the Workers' Statute, and in some cases operated cameras in breach of the authorisation limits. This made the processing unlawful under Article 5(1)(a) and Article 88 GDPR and Article 114 of the Italian Code. The Garante fined the company EUR 50,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A complainant found that the Belgian municipality Commune Y had consulted his national register record on 25 May 2022 and again on 10 November 2022. He emailed the municipality's data protection officer twice asking for an explanation, and received no reply to either email. The Chamber Contentieuse issued a prima facie decision, not a merits decision, finding the municipality may have breached the GDPR. It ordered the municipality to comply with the complainant's access request within 30 days and to report back to the Authority.
A controller who fails to respond to an access request due to an employee error is nonetheless liable for the violation of Article 15 GDPR.

Following one of noyb's 101 US transfer complaints, the Norwegian DPA has notified a controller of their intent to reprimand their former use of Google Analytics and consequent transfer of personal data to the US in violation of Article 44 GDPR, as they did not have sufficient supplementary measures in place.
The Spanish DPA imposed fines of €10,000 and €5,000 to a controller for partially responding to and ignoring several times a data subject’s requests in violation of Article 15 and Article 17 GDPR.

A parent asked the child welfare service in X municipality to delete the note, in his son's child welfare file, that the father belongs to a national minority (tater). The service refused. On 30 September 2022 the Norwegian Data Protection Authority (Datatilsynet) concluded that the service had not breached the Personal Data Act by refusing, after explaining the service's duty to document and archive and the right to erasure in GDPR Article 17. On appeal, the Privacy Appeals Board upheld that decision on 28 February 2023: the journal note must be kept under archival rules, and the ethnicity detail is necessary to understand the service's handling of the concern report. The complaint was rejected.
The Archbishop should now make clear that all personal data collected and recorded and otherwise processed for the purposes of the administration of sacraments is permanently retained.

As part of a joint Baltic preventive inspection of short-term vehicle rental firms, the Latvian DPA sent the company two information requests (July and November 2022). The company never answered or explained why. The DPA found it had deliberately and continuously failed to provide information needed for the DPA's tasks, breaching Article 58(1)(e) GDPR and the Article 83(5)(e) offence. It set the fine at EUR 1,000 instead of the EUR 14,787.78 it had calculated, because the company made a loss in 2021 and the larger fine would risk insolvency.

The Irish DPC investigated Bank of Ireland Group plc after it notified ten personal data breaches on its Banking365 online banking platform between January and May 2020, in which customers' account data was wrongly disclosed to third parties. The DPC found that BOI infringed the integrity and confidentiality principle in Article 5(1)(f) GDPR and Article 32(1) GDPR by failing to put appropriate technical and organisational measures in place. It ordered BOI to bring its processing into compliance, issued a reprimand, and imposed a fine of EUR 750,000 for the Article 5(1)(f) infringement only.
The DPA fined SUPERCOR, S.A. €70,000 for installing video surveillance cameras in a staff break room used by employees without proper notice or consent.

The Italian DPA inspected Ediscom, a marketing company holding a database of 21 million people used for SMS and email campaigns, after complaints. It found that Ediscom's own web portals used dark patterns to push users into giving marketing consents. It also found that data bought from third-party data brokers lacked documented valid consent, and that some complainants' data was still used after they objected. The Garante fined Ediscom EUR 300,000, issued two bans on processing and two warnings, and ordered publication of the decision.

Banca d'Italia sent eight mass emails to about 5,500 candidates in a public recruitment competition, to give COVID-19 safety instructions for a preselection test. In one of those emails, by mistake, the addresses of the recipients were placed in the visible To/cc field instead of blind copy, so recipients could see each other's addresses. The Garante found that this disclosure to third parties had no legal basis and violated Articles 5(1)(a) and 6 GDPR, along with Article 2-ter of the Italian Code. It issued a reprimand and no fine, treating the case as a minor violation caused by an isolated human error.

Problem Solving, a Vodafone telemarketing partner, acquired about 4.3 million contact records from two list providers (Ad-Opera and BR Pharma) and passed them to Vodafone for promotional campaigns. The Garante found that the company acted as an autonomous controller for this acquisition and communication, yet gave data subjects no information notice of its own and obtained no consent for the disclosure. It found breaches of Articles 13, 5(1)(a), 6 and 7 GDPR. It banned further processing of the data from the two providers, ordered a compliant list-acquisition procedure, and fined the company EUR 54,609.62, equal to 2% of its turnover. The decision is also published on the Garante's website.
The Italian DPA found that the publication of mugshots by an online newspaper was unfair and unlawful under Article 5(1)(a) GDPR.
The Slovenian DPA fined a perpetrator €320 for examining and taking photos of data subjects’ identity cards without any legal basis.

An employee of a Belgian municipality complained that the municipality used GPS tracking on service vehicles and used the location data in a note accusing him of clocking-in fraud. The Litigation Chamber found that the municipality had no valid legal basis for the geolocation processing and could not show accountability for it. It also found cookie consent defects, transparency and record-keeping failures, and a DPO reporting failure, most of which the municipality had partly remedied. Because the defendant is a public body, the Chamber said it could not impose an administrative fine, and it issued a reprimand and dismissed the remaining findings.
The Austrian DPA refused to act on a complaint and declared it “dishonest” and “abusive” after a data subject asked a controller to pay €2,900 for GDPR violations as an alternative to litigation.

A Vodafone subscriber complained that, after requesting access to her recorded calls, she received through a processor a CD containing another customer's calls, and that Vodafone did nothing to investigate after she told it. The HDPA found a breach of the right of access (Art. 15) and of the obligation to notify a personal data breach (Art. 33). It ordered Vodafone to satisfy the access request by sending the correct recordings and imposed a fine of EUR 40,000.

A former employee complained that her employer's staff intranet announced her dismissal and stated that the employer had ended her contract with immediate effect. The Chambre Contentieuse held that the announcement of the departure itself was lawful, but that naming which party ended the contract and whether the termination was immediate was not necessary for informing staff, and was sensitive data. It found breaches of Article 5(1)(a) and 6(1) GDPR (no valid lawful basis for that mention) and Article 5(1)(c) GDPR (data minimisation). The decision is a prima facie decision, not a merits decision: it orders removal of the mention and issues a warning, with no fine.

In November 2021 the Data Protection Ombudsman ordered the credit information company Suomen Asiakastieto to change how it recorded payment default entries based on final court judgments and to delete the wrongly recorded entries. The company did not delete them, saying this was impossible. The Sanctions Board found that this was non-compliance with a supervisory authority order and treated it as deliberate. It fined the company EUR 440,000 under Articles 58(2)(i) and 83(6) GDPR. The decision is not final and can be appealed to the administrative court.

A complainant wrote three letters to the King asking for help in a dispute with a federal agency and the German-speaking Community Government. The King's Office forwarded one of them (of 5 July 2019) to the Community Government, and the complainant objected that this had no lawful basis and that his access request and information rights were ignored. The Chamber found the forwarding lawful under Article 6(1)(e) GDPR and found no violation of Article 5(1)(a) or 6(1). It found that the controller breached Articles 12 and 13 by not informing the complainant, and ordered compliance, but no fine could be imposed because of the immunity the controller enjoys. The access request was held not to be a valid Article 15 request.

The DPA ruled that publishing coowners' personal data on a notice board requires a lawful basis under Article 6 GDPR. Doing so without one violates privacy by making it publicly available to non-owners.

The complainant asked two lenders on 8 June 2022 for access to her personal data under Article 15 GDPR, including information on any transfers to debt collection companies. Neither lender answered within one month, and no extension was notified or justified. The Chamber Contentieuse issued a prima facie decision, not a decision on the merits, finding the lenders may have infringed Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 15(1) GDPR. It ordered them to comply with the access request within 30 days and to report back by email.

The Belgian DPA ordered a controller to comply with an objection and erasure request pursuant to Article 58(2)(c) GDPR. The DPA determined that the controller should also order recipients to erase the data.

A hotel guest complained that on arrival at the hotel in August 2021 a receptionist photocopied his COVID-19 vaccination certificate and kept the copy, which was destroyed only later. The Authority found that storing the vaccination data in a filing system breached the principles of lawfulness, fairness and transparency under Article 5(1)(a), read with Article 13, because the guest was not informed as required. The Authority issued a reprimand to the hotel company. The complaint about access and erasure rights was dismissed as too vague.

The Latvian data protection authority (DVI) was investigating the company's apparent processing of voice data in audio-recording form. It sent the company information requests in 2022 (1 September and 22 November), and the company did not reply within the deadlines or explain why. The official found the company guilty of failing to provide information to the DVI under section 3(4) of the Latvian Administrative Penalties Law and imposed a fine of EUR 800 (160 fine units), below the middle of the statutory range. The fine is a national administrative sanction, not a GDPR Article 83 fine, and the decision can be challenged by complaint to the DVI director.

A complainant asked the controller to erase his email address, which it used for unsolicited marketing, on 9 and 14 November 2022. The controller confirmed on the second request that it would act, but the complainant still received marketing emails on 16 January 2023. The Litigation Chamber found infringements of Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 17(1) GDPR. It issued a prima facie order under Article 58(2)(c) GDPR and Article 95 of the Belgian DPA Act to comply with the erasure request within 30 days. This is not a decision on the merits, and the controller may request a merits hearing within 30 days.

A former employee complained that his employer, a transport company, gave his personal data to the German Federal Office for Goods Transport as the driver responsible for a toll violation on 15.09.2020. On that date he was on sick leave and the truck had already been handed to another lessee. The company said an employee made an involuntary mistake with dates. The Commission found that disclosure had no legal basis under Art. 6(1) and breached the principles of Art. 5(1)(a) and (b). It imposed a fine of BGN 10,000 on the company.

A complainant could only access guloggratis.dk by consenting to personal data processing or by paying 29 DKK per month. The Danish DPA examined whether this consent mechanism was freely given. It found that the cookie-wall alternative was acceptable in principle, but that the company had not shown that processing for statistical purposes was a necessary part of the paid alternative. The DPA issued an order to demonstrate this or to offer separate consent for statistics, with a compliance deadline of 8 March 2023, and expressed no criticism.

A data subject complained that the news website jv.dk allowed access to only some unlocked articles against consent to cookies for statistics and marketing, or to all content by paying a subscription. The Danish DPA held that this set-up did not give visitors a real free choice, so the consent was not freely given and the processing was not lawful. It also held that the publisher had not shown that processing for statistical purposes was necessary for the paid alternative. The DPA ordered the publisher to make its consent valid and to be able to demonstrate it, with a compliance deadline of 8 March 2023, but issued no criticism and no fine.

Romania's data protection authority finished an investigation in January 2023 into Medijobs Platform SRL, which had notified a personal data breach. Unauthorised access to its IT infrastructure allowed some candidate CV data to be downloaded and deleted. The authority found that the company had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational security measures, and fined it RON 24,610.5 (EUR 5,000). It also ordered the company to review and update its security measures, procedures and staff training.

The Polish DPA opened proceedings on its own initiative after a notified personal data breach in which unauthorised persons obtained access to and downloaded the data of 2,494 customers, including PESEL numbers and health data. It found that the controller, a sole trader, had not implemented adequate technical and organisational measures. It also found that the controller had not checked whether its processor gave sufficient guarantees, and that the processing agreement lacked mandatory elements. The controller was fined PLN 33,012 (about EUR 7,000) and ordered to stop entrusting processing to the processor under that agreement. The processor, also a sole trader, was found to have infringed Article 32 and Article 28(3) and was fined PLN 472 (about EUR 100).

A person who records their abusive partner and shares the evidence with the police has a legitimate interest to do so. There is (obviously) no need to inform the ex-partner beforehand, the Icelandic DPA held.

Datatilsynet received several complaints between 2018 and 2021 against the fitness chain SATS about how it handled access and erasure requests. It examined them together as lead authority under the one-stop-shop mechanism. It found that SATS answered two access requests late, did not erase data promptly after three erasure requests, did not properly inform banned members about retention and its legal basis, and had no valid lawful basis for processing members' training history. It imposed an administrative fine of NOK 10 million, about 0.3% of SATS' 2021 turnover and about 5% of the maximum applicable fine.

A person complained that Epic Ltd, a telecoms and TV provider, kept calling his phone number after he had left the company as a customer. The company explained that a list of current customers used for upselling calls had wrongly included 332 former customers because of a date-entry error, and that calls were made to them in April 2021. The Commissioner found breaches of the GDPR's lawfulness rule and of the controller's accountability and organisational-measures duties, and imposed a fine of EUR 3,250 instead of the reprimand the company had requested.

The complainant found that Y had consulted his national register record on 12 September 2022. On 25 September 2022 he emailed Y's privacy address asking why and by whom, but the mailbox was full and the email was never received, so Y did not reply within one month. The Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision, not a merits decision, finding that Y may have failed to facilitate the exercise of data subject rights. It ordered Y to comply with the access request within 30 days and to confirm compliance by email.

The Danish Data Protection Agency investigated, on its own motion after a citizen's complaint, how Statens Serum Institut (SSI) meets its duty to inform people whose data it did not collect directly. SSI argued that individual notification would be disproportionately burdensome given its sample volumes and IT system. The Agency found that SSI cannot rely on the Article 14(5)(b) exemption to skip the Article 14(1)-(3) duty for samples received for analysis, nor the Article 14(4) duty for residual material kept in the Danish National Biobank. No fine was imposed; SSI was ordered to report within three months on how it will meet Article 14.

A new Vodafone prepaid subscriber had expressly objected to the use of his data for marketing. He nevertheless received a parcel of promotional product samples from an advertising company, Chapter Five, to which Vodafone had passed his name, address and phone number. Vodafone argued the parcel was a welcome gift incidental to the contract, not marketing. The Authority found the processing and transfer unlawful, unfair and non-transparent, and incompatible with the original purpose, and that Article 13 information was not shown to have been given. It fined Vodafone EUR 10,000 and ordered it to adapt its practice within one month so that such extra benefits come with full information and a right to object.

A bank customer complained that Piraeus Bank gave a third party, his opponent in a court case, the detailed transactions of two bank accounts he held jointly with his late aunt. The bank admitted that an employee, by mistake and against instructions, handed the data to an heir of the aunt without noticing the accounts were joint and without asking the legal department. The bank did not notify the breach to the Authority or to the customer, arguing that human error is not a breach caused by inadequate security measures. The Authority found breaches of lawfulness and confidentiality principles and of the breach notification and communication duties, and imposed a total fine of EUR 30,000.

The Garante acted after press reports of tests showing risks for minors and emotionally vulnerable users of the Replika AI chatbot. It found that the app had no age verification, no blocking mechanism when users declared they were underage, and a privacy policy that did not disclose the essential elements of the processing, including the use of children's data. On that basis it found breaches of Articles 5, 6, 8, 9 and 25 GDPR (and of Article 13 on transparency), and urgently ordered a temporary limitation of the processing of the personal data of users in Italy under Article 58(2)(f). The Garante reserved further decisions pending the outcome of its investigation.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in January 2023 into Tensa Art Design SA after a data subject complained about constant unsolicited messages. The company kept sending commercial emails to the person even though they had repeatedly unsubscribed from the newsletter and objected. The authority found a breach of Article 21(3) GDPR and fined the company RON 4,927.3 (about EUR 1,000). It also ordered the company to change its procedures so that data subjects' rights are always respected.

After a complaint from a patient, the Romanian authority investigated a dental clinic (Dent Estet Clinic SA) and a collaborating dentist. Photos and X-rays of the patient's orthodontic treatment, linkable to the patient's name, were published in a blog article for scientific and commercial purposes. The clinic was told of the unauthorised disclosure by the patient but did not notify the authority within 72 hours, breaching Art. 33 GDPR. It was fined RON 4,919.2 (about EUR 1,000) and given a corrective measure. The dentist was separately fined the same amount under Arts. 6, 9 and 12-14 GDPR.
The use of Cloudflare violates Art. 44 DSGVO.

A co-owner of a house in Sofia complained that his brother, another co-owner, had installed three CCTV cameras covering shared areas (basement, yard and staircase) without consent. The Commission found that the controller, who holds a two-thirds share, could lawfully decide on the property's protection, that the cameras covered only common areas and were signposted, and that the surveillance was justified by property protection and the safety of a minor child. It declared the complaint unfounded.

A health authority (ULSS n.5 Polesana) notified a personal data breach: a copy of a patient's medical record handed to him contained 30 pages of another patient's clinical documentation. The Garante found the disclosure of health data had no legal basis and that security measures were inadequate. It took into account that only one patient was affected, the error was human and happened in the Covid emergency, the authority cooperated and acted promptly. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision; no corrective orders were imposed.

A person complained that the hospital authority had sent him a medical report belonging to another patient. The inquiry showed that counter staff of the blood-collection centre were emailing lab reports on request without the encryption and password protection required by the 2013 Prime Ministerial Decree, contrary to the hospital's own instructions. The Garante found the processing of health data unlawful (Arts. 5, 9, 32 GDPR and Art. 75 of the Code) and fined the hospital EUR 7,000, noting the Covid-19 context, its cooperation and its remedial steps. No corrective measures were ordered, and the decision is published in full.

An employee of the municipality of Misterbianco complained that the municipality published on its online notice board a determination, with annexed rankings, on a pay-progression procedure. It disclosed her and other employees' personal data, including details of a labour court judgment and a repayment by salary deductions of up to one fifth. The Garante found the online dissemination had no adequate legal basis and breached the GDPR principles and the Italian Code. It fined the municipality EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website. No corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

Three individuals complained that a political party had included their names and personal ID numbers in the list of supporters submitted to the Central Election Commission to register for the 4 April 2021 parliamentary elections. Handwriting expert reports found the signatures were not theirs, so the data was processed without consent and without any other Article 6(1) basis. The party did not take part in the proceedings or provide the requested evidence. The Commission found the complaints well founded and fined the party BGN 25,000 for breaching Article 6(1) GDPR. It also ordered the party to adopt organisational measures, training and a data protection policy for breaching Articles 24 and 5(2).

A individual, through his lawyer, complained that two online newspaper articles from 2014 about a judicial investigation still appeared under his name in search results, even though he was acquitted by a final 2019 judgment. He had asked both publishers to delete the data in December 2019. The Garante declared the complaint well-founded and ordered Il Sole 24 Ore and SEIF to take technical measures to stop external search engines indexing the articles against his name. It also issued a warning to both publishers for failing to properly answer the erasure request, which is a breach of Article 12 in substance. No fine was imposed.

A complainant asked the controller to erase his email address, which was used to send him unsolicited direct marketing. The controller did not erase it and instead asked for other email addresses linked to the complainant, which the Litigation Chamber found went beyond data minimisation. The Chamber found prima facie breaches of Articles 5(1)(c), 5(2), 12(2) and 17(1) GDPR. It ordered the controller to comply with the erasure request within 30 days and to report the result, failing which the case would proceed to a merits hearing. No fine was imposed.

A complaint was lodged against a company over disclosure of an employee's personal data from his employment contract. In the complaint proceedings the Polish DPA twice asked the company for explanations, and the company never replied. The DPA opened separate ex officio proceedings and found a breach of the duty to cooperate (Art. 31) and of the duty to give the authority information and access (Art. 58(1)(a) and (e)). It imposed a fine of PLN 18,279 (about EUR 4,000). The breach was treated as intentional and continuing, and the company did not respond even to the notice of the fine proceedings.

A data subject complained that the company had not properly fulfilled his right of access, even after the Inspectorate had ordered it to provide the Article 15 information in June 2022. The company's reply was brief and generic: it gave no detailed legal basis, no recipients, and no source information, and it did not provide a copy of the data. The Inspectorate found infringements of the transparency principle and of Article 15(1)(a), (b), (c), (d), (g) and 15(3) GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 8,000, treating the breach as medium in seriousness, continuing and intentional, and noting that the company had not complied with the earlier order.

The Irish DPC conducted an own-volition inquiry into Centric Health after a data breach in which health records of about 70,000 patients became unavailable for two days and records of about 2,500 were permanently deleted. It found that Centric infringed Articles 5(1)(f), 5(2) and 32(1) GDPR through inadequate security measures and failure to demonstrate accountability. The DPC issued a reprimand and three administrative fines totalling €460,000.

The Dutch DPA fined the Social Insurance Institution (SVB) EUR 150,000 for not having appropriate technical and organisational measures to secure personal data in telephone contact with state pension (AOW) clients. The case began with a complaint and a breach notification in 2019, when a relative received a client's information from an SVB employee. The AP found that identity checks and risk assessment were inadequate, and that the infringement ran from 25 May 2018 until June 2022. The standard fine for this category was EUR 310,000. It was lowered because of mitigating circumstances and again, on proportionality grounds, because the SVB acted quickly to fix the problem. No order under penalty was imposed because the infringement had already been ended.

The Swedish DPA (IMY) examined two erasure requests sent to Lensway Group AB in 2020 by complainants referred from Finland and Denmark. The company required a copy of an identity document and a signature, and asked that the documents be sent by ordinary post. IMY found that the ID copy and signature were not necessary to confirm the identities, and that requiring postal submission did not facilitate the exercise of the right to erasure. IMY issued a reprimand rather than a fine, because the infringements were minor and the company no longer requests ID copies or signatures for erasure requests.

A complainant received an e-mail from the insurer If Skadeförsäkring AB on 6 November 2020 containing a medical assessment, sent with enforced TLS encryption that did not cover the whole route to the recipient. IMY found that If had not ensured an appropriate level of security under Article 32(1) GDPR, because the encryption ended at the recipient's operator server and was not end-to-end. Considering the infringement minor and the remedial steps taken, IMY issued a reprimand under Article 58(2)(b) instead of a fine.

Someone at the District Court Szczecin-Centrum (the decision does not say who) lost three USB drives, two of them private and unencrypted, holding draft judgments and reasoning from 2004 to 2020, including names, addresses, workplaces and health data. The court reported the breach to the UODO. The UODO found that the court had not blocked USB ports or unregistered media, although its own risk analysis and audits had recommended this, and had only imposed a formal ban on private media. It found breaches of the confidentiality and accountability principles and of the security and data protection by design duties, and fined the court PLN 30,000. The part of the case concerning storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)) was discontinued because the UODO has no competence over the exercise of the administration of justice.

A complainant asked the controller on 1 December 2022 to erase his personal data under Article 17(1) GDPR, and sent a reminder on 19 December 2022. He had no answer by 3 January 2023, although he received a promotional email from the controller on 28 December 2022. The Litigation Chamber found, on a prima facie basis, that the controller breached Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 17(1) GDPR. It ordered the controller to comply with the erasure request within 30 days and to report the result to the authority. The decision is not a decision on the merits, and the controller may ask for a merits hearing within 30 days.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in December 2022 into Dante Internațional SA, owner of emag.ro, after a data subject complained that his right to erasure was not respected. The company sent a commercial SMS to the complainant's phone although he had earlier asked for his account and data to be deleted. The authority found a breach of Article 17 GDPR and fined the company RON 4,918.6 (about EUR 1,000). It also ordered the company to adopt technical and organisational measures to act effectively on data subject requests, including erasure.

The Spanish DPA fined a private detective €2,000 because of a violation of Article 13 GDPR. The data subject was not informed how her personal data would be processed. The website of the detective, which was referred to in the contract with the data subject, lacked a privacy notice.

The Garante issued an urgent provisional limitation order against GMC – Giuseppe Marra Communications S.p.A, the operator of adnkronos.com. An article published on 16 January 2023 gave detailed information about one identified person's illness and reproduced a full, highly detailed laboratory report. The order bars further dissemination of that health data, including the report, and of similar information in other articles on the site, with immediate effect on receipt. The Garante reserved all further decisions until its investigation is complete, and it noted that non-compliance carries criminal and administrative sanctions.

The Italian DPA issued an urgent provisional order against Suditaly Imprese Meridionali Società Cooperativa, the controller of the online news outlet Dayitalianews. The outlet had published a detailed article about one identified person's illness, including a full laboratory test report. The Garante found that disclosing this health data conflicted with the Italian Code and the journalism code of conduct, and it ordered a temporary limitation on further dissemination of the health data, including in other articles on the same site. The controller had 3 days to report measures taken. No fine was imposed; the investigation was still open.

The Italian DPA took urgent action after the online newspaper PalermoToday published an article giving detailed news of a named person's illness, with a full copy of a very detailed laboratory report attached. The Garante ordered Citynews S.p.A., with immediate effect, a provisional limitation on further dissemination of the health data in the article and the attached report, and of any similar information in other articles on the same site. The order was made under Article 58(2)(f) GDPR, and the investigation remains open with all other decisions reserved.

The Italian DPA took an urgent provisional measure against Retimedia S.r.l., the publisher of the online newspaper La Cronaca24. An article had reported in detail on the illness of an identified person (named only as XX) and included a full, highly detailed laboratory report. The Garante ordered a provisional limitation on further dissemination of the health data in that article and of any similar information in other articles on the same site, with immediate effect. The company was required to report within 3 days on the steps taken, and the Garante reserved its final determination pending the investigation.

A municipal early-childhood education provider sent parents a questionnaire during the COVID-19 pandemic asking whether children would be cared for at home, and attached a notice. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found that the form and notice did not clearly tell parents the purpose of the data collection or its legal basis, and whether answering was voluntary or compulsory. The controller was given a reprimand (huomautus) under Article 58(2)(b) GDPR. No fine was imposed, and the decision was not yet final when it was given on 18 January 2023.

A patient complained after receiving a summons letter for a medical visit in a window envelope that showed the patient's name, address, the sender clinic and that it was a summons. IMY examined the summons mailings from three Region Dalarna clinics, which were sent by a postal service provider. It found that the committee had processed health data, including data on children, without appropriate security measures, in breach of Article 32(1) GDPR, from 6 May 2021 to 6 July 2022. IMY imposed an administrative fine of SEK 200,000.

The Bulgarian Commission for Personal Data Protection upheld a complaint from a data subject whose mobile number was ported to a telecom operator without her knowledge or consent, using an application she had not signed and an office visit she had not made. The operator argued the transfer was an error caused by her husband, but the Commission found that it processed her three names, national ID number and phone number without a legal basis, unfairly and non-transparently, and without adequate organisational measures or controls. The operator was fined BGN 2000 and ordered to bring its processing into line with the GDPR and to report back within three months.

The Irish DPC ran an own-volition inquiry into CCTV and ANPR surveillance run by Kildare County Council, covering traffic management, housing estates, litter enforcement and the sharing of footage with An Garda Síochána. It found several infringements of the GDPR and the Data Protection Act 2018, including unlawful processing without a legal basis and failures of security, transparency and data minimisation. It imposed one administrative fine of EUR 50,000, for failing to put up signage or give required information for the traffic management CCTV (Articles 13(1) and 13(3)), and no fine for the access-log failure under Article 32(1). It also imposed temporary bans and compliance orders.

The complainant in the case at hand (the husband) incurred an obligation to disclose his assets as well as income to his wife as a beneficiary of maintenance in the course of divorce proceedings. This did not lead to a violation of the complainant's right to confidentiality by the processing of his personal data.

The Cypriot Commissioner re-examined a 2018 complaint by two police investigators whose names and photographs were published by the newspaper Politis in a June 2018 article about an elderly woman's detention at Larnaca airport. The Commissioner's first decision (January 2019, a EUR 10,000 fine) was annulled by the Administrative Court in February 2022 for lack of a right to be heard, so the case was re-examined. The Commissioner now finds breaches of Article 5(1)(c) and Article 6(1)(f) GDPR and imposes a fine of EUR 7,000, reduced from the earlier amount because the article had been removed, a written apology published and the newspaper cooperated.

After press reports of spyware being used to monitor phones in Greece, the authority opened an investigation and carried out on-site inspections at the offices of Intellexa S.A., a company linked in the press to the Predator spyware. The registered office had no real operations and the second site was an empty building. The authority sent 24 written questions, but the company did not answer for over 40 days, and then only partly, leaving out information it plainly held. The authority found a breach of Article 31 GDPR (duty to cooperate with the supervisory authority), fined the company EUR 50,000 and ordered it to hand over the invoices, the material sent to the National Transparency Authority and its relevant contracts straight away.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in December 2022 into Bristol Logistics SA. The investigation began after the company sent two personal data breach notifications. A binder holding the personnel files of 12 employees was stolen, so unauthorised persons accessed the data. The authority found that the company had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational security measures, fined it RON 9,828 (about EUR 2,000), and ordered it to review and update its measures and to train authorised staff.

The Irish DPC announced the conclusion of its inquiry into WhatsApp Ireland, started by a complaint from a German data subject about 'forced consent' to updated Terms of Service. Following an EDPB binding determination of 5 December 2022, the DPC's final decision of 12 January 2023 found WhatsApp could not rely on the contract legal basis for service improvement and security, and also found transparency breaches (Articles 12, 13(1)(c) and 5(1)(a)). It fined WhatsApp Ireland €5.5 million for the Article 6(1) breach, no further fine being imposed for transparency as €225 million had already been imposed earlier. WhatsApp must bring its processing into compliance within six months. The complaint's forced-consent aspect was rejected.

The Latvian DVI examined LocateFamily, a website offering people-search for contact details, which published names, addresses and phone numbers of about 13,323 Latvian residents. LocateFamily argued that GDPR did not apply because it is not established in the EU and that the data came from public sources before GDPR, with consent implied. The DVI held that GDPR applies under Article 3(2), that no consent or other lawful basis under Article 6(1) existed, that the purpose limitation principle was breached, and that no EU representative had been appointed under Article 27(1). Instead of a fine, it ordered LocateFamily to delete the data of Latvian residents from the website and report to the DVI by 1 March 2023.

A complainant, through her lawyer, asked the Azienda Sanitaria Locale di Brindisi for access to her personal data and an explanation of an incorrect entry in her COVID-19 vaccination record. The ASL did not reply until the Authority asked it to. The Garante found a breach of Article 12(3) in conjunction with Article 15 GDPR, noting that the incorrect entry had already been deleted and that the ASL had apologised. It imposed a fine of EUR 2,500, ordered no corrective measures, and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

A teacher complained that the regional school office's Brescia branch published on its website a transfer decision containing personal information and the reason for his priority in mobility, namely assistance to a family member under Law 104/1992, which reveals health information. The office blacked out the health reference after the request but left the decision itself online with the teacher's data. The Garante found publication (dissemination) without a legal basis and in breach of lawfulness, minimisation and the ban on disseminating health data. It fined the office EUR 6,000, restricted further online dissemination of the complainant's data, required a report within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

A hospital-university trust in Padua sent an email to 19 heart-transplant waiting-list patients, asking for consent to a clinical study, with all addresses visible in the cc field instead of bcc. This revealed to each recipient that the others were patients awaiting a heart transplant. The trust notified the breach itself. The Garante found unlawful disclosure of health data in breach of Articles 5(1)(f) and 9 GDPR and fined the trust EUR 5,000. It imposed no corrective measures because the trust had already acted, and ordered publication of the decision.

A woman who had been involved in failed acquisition talks with the company complained that her individual business email account stayed active after the relationship ended and was accessed. The company kept the account open, forwarded incoming mail to its sales director and deactivated it only at the end of February 2019, citing its interest in serving prospective clients and in defending itself in a civil case. The Garante found the processing unlawful and the reply to her deletion request inadequate, breaching the principles of lawfulness, fairness and minimisation, the legal basis requirements, and the rules on transparency and data subject rights. It fined the company EUR 5,000 and ordered publication. The charges under Article 88 GDPR and Articles 113 and 114 of the Code were dropped.

The Garante inspected Commify Italia, which runs the Skebby SMS platform, in November 2021. It found the company kept the content of customers' SMS messages (including OTPs, health and political messages) without a valid legal basis, had weak security for traffic data (single-factor authentication, http API endpoints, no logging of operations on the systems), and scanned message content for fraud. It fined the company EUR 80,000 under the Art. 83(5) cap, issued two reprimands for the fraud scanning and for the Art. 25 failings, and ordered publication of the decision.

A former politician complained to the Garante that Google kept search results linking his name to news articles and a campaign video from his political period, almost ten years earlier. Google had removed one URL by manual measures, which the Garante noted, but refused to delist the others. The Garante upheld the complaint for the remaining URL, weighing the time elapsed, his having held no political office for five years, and the absence of a current information need. It ordered Google to delist the result within twenty days and recorded the measure in its internal register, without treating that entry as a precedent for future fines. No fine was imposed.

A magistrate who is a member of the National Association of Magistrates complained that the association sent a confidential notice of internal disciplinary proceedings to the general certified email address of the prosecutor's office where he works, rather than his personal address. Staff of the office therefore saw the information and it was handed to him by hand. The Garante found a breach of the integrity and confidentiality principle and of Articles 25 and 32. It fined the association EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision, but did not impose a corrective order because the association had already changed its practice.

After Google failed to respond to a right to erasure request made by a Greek data subject, the Greek DPA held that it is competent to examine the complaint, as the processing concerns only a Greek data subject, and is conducted by Google LLC, based in the US.

The Catalan DPA found that the principles of GDPR do not limit the right to access public information on the number of gender transition cases in Catalonia broken down by sex, age, and year because of the efficient anonymisation of the data.

A Austrian filmmaker complained that Wikimedia Foundation Inc. refused his request of 29 June 2018 to erase his Wikipedia biography, relying on the right to erasure under Article 17 GDPR. The foundation argued that the GDPR did not apply to it and, alternatively, that journalistic and public-interest reasons applied. The DSB dismissed the complaint as unfounded: the applicant is a person in public life, the information is accurate and widely available, and the public's interest in access to information outweighs his interest, so the exception in Article 17(3)(a) applies and there was no violation of the right to erasure.

After a complaint by the Norwegian Humanist Association on behalf of eight data subjects, the Norwegian DPA examined the Church of Norway's use of birth notifications for members' children obtained from the population register. Between 1 October and 14 November 2018, after the church's legal access to these confidential records had lapsed, the church kept collecting and storing them without a valid legal basis under Article 6. The church also failed to give the required information under Article 14, read with Article 12(1). The DPA issued a reprimand under Article 58(2)(b) and imposed no fine.

Datatilsynet received two breach notifications from PostNord AS. In both cases, people who received a reassigned phone number could log into the mypostnord customer profile of the previous owner and see personal data. Datatilsynet found that PostNord's risk assessment was inadequate and that phone-number-only authentication did not ensure adequate confidentiality, so PostNord violated Article 32 GDPR. It ordered PostNord to identify the risks and implement suitable technical measures; no fine was imposed.

The Spanish DPA issued a reprimand and determined that the Island Council of El Hierro adjust the publications on its transparency portal, reconciling its obligation to publish acts of public interest with the protection of personal data.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in December 2022 into the water utility Apă Canal Ilfov SA after the company notified a personal data breach. When emailing users registered on its online portal, the company put the recipients' email addresses in the 'To' field instead of 'BCC', so addresses were disclosed to other recipients and a significant number of people were affected. The authority found that the company had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational security measures. It fined the company RON 14,757.60 (stated as equivalent to EUR 3,000) for breaching Article 32(1)(b), 32(2) and 32(4) GDPR.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation into a homeowners' association in Iași after a complaint that it posted payment lists with members' full names and a defamatory notice naming the complainant. It found the association disclosed the complainant's name on the notice board without consent or another legal basis. It imposed a fine of RON 2,462.5 (about EUR 500) and a warning for the breach of Article 6, plus a corrective measure to ensure processing complies with the GDPR.

A newspaper article reports that the Sachsen-Anhalt data protection commissioner fined Magdeburg University Hospital EUR 9,000 for concealing serious data protection violations. An employee is said to have misused the hospital's access to population registers to retrieve personal data of uninvolved people. The hospital board kept this from the authority for over a year. A further EUR 450 was charged for the costs of the proceedings. The article is paywalled, so only the opening paragraphs are available.

Employees of a company complained, through their lawyer, that the CEO had accessed audio recorded by the reception CCTV camera on his own mobile phone and that his PA had the same access to the cameras. The company's own CCTV Policy said the cameras would not record sound. The Commissioner watched the video supplied by the complainants and found that the camera did record audio and that the complainants could be identified. The company gave only late and limited submissions and did not answer the complainants' rebuttal. The Commissioner found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 5(1)(b), 5(1)(c) and 6 GDPR and fined the company EUR 5,000. The company was also ordered to stop the cameras recording audio and to put up signs informing people about the cameras.

A parent complained that a public therapy service for children had ignored or delayed her access request for her minor son's occupational and speech therapy file, made on 24 May 2022 and met only on 30 June 2022. The Commissioner found that the controller was the department itself, not its Director, and that the request sent to the child's therapists was a valid request. It found failures to reply within one month, to give the information and a copy of the data, to involve the DPO in time, and to provide a compliant privacy policy and an internal data protection notice. It ordered the policy to be revised and an internal notice adopted within 60 days, reminded the controller about staff training, and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 2,500.

In its 2023 annual report the Baden-Württemberg data protection authority describes a case in which a hospital employee, whose job was billing, used the hospital's patient administration system to look up her new neighbour. She could see the neighbour's full personal details, all hospital stays and diagnoses. The authority fined her EUR 2,000 as a natural person. In setting the amount it took into account that it was a first offence, that she also faced employment-law consequences, and that the data were special-category data under Art. 9 GDPR. The hospital helped clear up the facts and took employment-law steps itself.

In its 2023 annual report the Baden-Württemberg data protection authority describes fines on public-sector employees who used official databases for private reasons. One police employee ran several queries in the MeldIT registration portal after a radio report made her curious about the people involved. The authority fined her EUR 1,200 as effective, dissuasive and proportionate. The report explains that the ban on fining public bodies does not protect employees who act on their own initiative for private purposes. The report does not name the individual.

The 2023 annual report of the Bremen data protection commissioner has a short section on a fine imposed on a clinic. Prompted by a complaint, the authority fined the clinic for sending an unredacted psychiatric treatment report on a patient to an accident insurance fund without any legal basis. The report said the discharge report held extensive information on health, criminal allegations and other private matters, seriously infringed the patient's personality rights, and threatened disadvantages in the assessment of his accident pension. The report gives no amount for this fine and no decision date.

The Bremen data protection authority's 6th annual report (covering 2023) describes five fines imposed on a real estate agency (Maklerbüro). The agency repeatedly called and emailed a former customer of its predecessor office, a property prospect, to ask about property interest, even after he objected and asked for erasure of his data. The authority found the agency had no legal basis for the contact and that it should have erased all his data once he asked. The report gives no article numbers, no amount for these fines and no date for this case.

The Bremen data protection authority's 2023 annual report describes a fine on the operator of a dating internet platform for violating Article 32 GDPR. The platform had no e-mail verification at registration, so a third party could register using a data subject's e-mail address, and the data subject then received registration confirmations and platform messages. The case came to the authority through a complaint. The report gives no amount for this fine.

This is the Bremen data protection authority's annual report for 2023, covering many fines. Section 4.7 says that in five cases the authority fined website operators for using the tracking tool Google Analytics without the visitors' prior consent. The report gives no amount for these five fines and does not name any operator.

In its 2023 annual report the Hamburg data protection authority describes administrative fine proceedings against an unnamed company based in Hamburg. A complainant had to report his sick leave by email to a distribution list of 25 people, many of whom did not work with him. His supervisor also sent an email to a large group of colleagues listing all his sick days. The authority found that this disclosure of health data breached Art. 32 and Art. 9 GDPR and fined the company EUR 75,000. It counted the company's extensive cooperation and a compensation payment to the complainant in its favour, and the fact that health data was involved against it. The company accepted the fine and waived its right to object.

The annual report describes a fine against an employee of a credit institution who, while live-streaming a video game on Twitch, used access rights granted by his employer to look up personal data of an opposing player in order to visit that player at home. The authority treated him as the controller because he used business resources for private purposes (employee excess). It imposed a fine in the mid four-figure range, taking into account his estimated economic situation and the intentional nature of the act. He accepted the fine and the notice is final. The report gives no exact amount, no GDPR articles and no date for this case.

In its 2023 annual report the Hamburg data protection authority describes a fine against a daycare center. The center had thrown binders of personal data about children and their parents into a publicly accessible waste-paper container. The binders held childcare contracts with account data, vaccination records, health check results and copies of ID documents. A member of the public found them and the center refused to fix the problem, so the authority was called in. It found a breach of Art. 32(1) GDPR and imposed a fine in the low four-figure range. The report gives no exact amount. The center accepted the fine and the decision is final.

After a complaint, the Brandenburg authority learned that the manager of an owner-run food store had pinned a table of sick days for 50 named employees for 2022 in the break room. The table stayed up for four weeks and was also accessible to third parties such as suppliers. The authority held that disclosing the absence reasons breached Art. 6(1) in conjunction with Art. 9(1) GDPR, because they were health data. It imposed a fine in the five-figure range, which the company accepted. The report does not give the exact amount.

The Brandenburg data protection authority's 2023 annual report describes a fine against an angling club. The club's website let anyone retrieve member lists with names, full addresses, phone numbers, birth dates and bank account details. A former board member had uploaded the files, and no legal basis allowed publishing them, so the authority found a breach of Art. 6 GDPR. It imposed a fine in the mid three-figure range under Art. 83(5)(a). The report gives no exact amount. The authority weighed the scope of the data and the number of people affected against the club's cooperation, its immediate takedown of the pages and its low annual turnover.

The 52nd annual report of the Hessian data protection commissioner describes a case against two doctors who ran a joint medical practice. The practice repeatedly threw its waste, including patient documents, into a publicly accessible paper container. The documents were only shredded in a way that left them easy to reconstruct, and some patient files were thrown away whole. The commissioner fined the two practice owners a total of EUR 3,600 for breaching Art. 5(1)(f) in conjunction with Art. 32(1)(b) GDPR. The fine was reduced because the doctors admitted the incident, took prompt corrective action and cooperated. It was increased because the breach was intentional, systematic and lasted several months, and it exposed sensitive health data. The owners accepted the fine notices and paid at once.

A company, which is not named in the report, kept sending advertising to a former customer even after he had objected to advertising. It had already received a warning in 2022 for ignoring the same person's objections. Its internal measures did not ensure that data records with different spellings of names and addresses were blocked for advertising. The Hessian commissioner found a negligent breach of the right to object (Art. 21(3) GDPR) and imposed a fine of EUR 25,000. The company lodged an objection (Einspruch) and the proceedings had not yet become final at the time of the report.

In its 2023 annual report, the Hessian data protection commissioner describes a case in which a company refused to cooperate while a data subject's complaint was being handled. The company ignored all letters, formal decisions, requests for information and instructions. The commissioner found a breach of the duty to cooperate under Art. 31 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 under Art. 83(4)(a) GDPR. The company had not paid the coercive penalties or the fine, so they were being collected through enforcement. The company is not named in the report.

The Bavarian data protection authority's 2023 annual report, in its chapter on the central fines office, describes several fines. One of them was a fine notice against a store detective. He first collected the contact details of a woman accused of shoplifting in his job, and then used them to contact her privately. The report gives no amount, no articles and no date for this case; it only says that fine notices were issued against employees in two such cases. It reports about EUR 3.8 million in fines in total for 2023.

The 13th annual report of the Bavarian data protection supervisory authority, covering 2023, describes the fines imposed by its central fines office. One example is a physician who answered a patient's online review and disclosed the patient's health data in a publicly visible reply. The public prosecutor had closed its own investigation, so the authority could pursue the case under the GDPR. The report says only that the fine was in the four-figure range. It names neither the physician nor an exact amount nor the specific articles for this case.

The Lower Saxony data protection authority's 2023 annual report describes fines it imposed after inspecting real estate firms. One company with turnover of around EUR 10 million was fined EUR 16,600 after a discussion procedure with the administrative authority. The reasons were missing joint controllership agreements, collecting and further processing personal data without a legal basis (6 data subjects), and not deleting personal data in time (3 data subjects). The report does not cite article numbers for this fine, and it names neither the company nor a specific decision date.

The Irish DPC inquired into a complaint, referred by the Austrian DPA, about Facebook's 2018 updated Terms of Service, the legal basis for processing and the transparency of information given to users. The decision follows a binding EDPB decision (Article 65) that changed the Commission's draft findings. The DPC found infringements of the transparency principle (Articles 5(1)(a), 12(1) and 13(1)(c)) and of Article 6(1) GDPR, and ordered Facebook to bring its processing into compliance. It imposed a total administrative fine of €210 million, made up of three separate fines.

The Irish DPC decided, after a complaint about the Instagram Terms of Use and the legal basis information given to users, that Meta Ireland failed to give sufficient information on processing relying on Article 6(1)(b) GDPR, failed to present that information transparently, and relied wrongly on Article 6(1)(b) for behavioural advertising, in line with the EDPB's binding decision. It ordered Meta Ireland to bring its processing into compliance within three months and imposed fines totalling EUR 180 million (EUR 70m, EUR 60m and EUR 50m for the three groups of infringements).

The Polish DPA was handling a complaint about disclosure of a complainant's data to unauthorised parties by a financial intermediation company. The company did not collect two registered letters requesting explanations, nor answer the letter opening the fine proceedings or a phone call with its president. The DPA opened proceedings on its own initiative and found a breach of Article 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR for failing to give it the information it needed.
