It imposed a fine of PLN 27,418 (stated as equal to EUR 6,000), treating the breach as intentional, continuing and a repeat of earlier non-cooperation that had drawn a reprimand.

The CNIL's restricted committee fined a company (the published decision withholds its name; the name on this page comes from the CNIL press release) for breaching Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act, which transposes the ePrivacy rules on storing or reading information on users' terminals. The case followed a complaint by an association that the personalised advertising setting on the company's devices was enabled by default, so users could not validly consent. The committee imposed an administrative fine of EUR 8 million and ordered publication of the decision, with the company's name removed after two years.

The CNIL restricted committee found that a mobile game publisher read the IDFV device identifier on iOS and sent it to advertising domains without the user's consent, which breaches Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act (the ePrivacy transposition). It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 3,000,000, ordered the company to obtain consent before using IDFV for advertising, set a penalty of EUR 20,000 per day of delay after three months, and ordered publication of the decision with the company's name removed after two years.
The French DPA fined TikTok €5,000,000 for implementing advertising identifiers on users' devices without prior consent. TikTok's cookie banner was also found insufficiently informative.

The Spanish DPA fined an electricity and gas company €24,000 for the lack of a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR to process the personal data of its client which was caused by an internal error in registering the data subject's will to enter into contract.

ANSPDCP completed an investigation at Kaufland România SCS in November 2022. A store manager let an employee into the CCTV monitoring room; the employee filmed the footage with a personal phone and sent it via WhatsApp to a third party, after which it was published by an online newspaper. The footage showed a person and a car registration number, affecting two data subjects. The authority found breaches of Articles 29 and 32 GDPR and fined the controller RON 14,779.80 (about EUR 3,000). It also ordered the controller to issue instructions banning employees from using personal devices to film, photograph or share CCTV recordings via WhatsApp or social media.

Following five complaints lodged between May 2018 and February 2019, the Finnish Data Protection Ombudsman's Sanctions Board found that a wellness-device company (anonymised as company X) processed health data such as heart rate, maximum oxygen uptake and BMI without valid explicit consent, as its consent request was general and not specific. The company was fined EUR 122,000 and given a reprimand, and was ordered to bring its processing into compliance with the GDPR. The case was handled under the one-stop-shop cooperation procedure, and the decision can be appealed to the administrative court and was not yet final at publication.
The Maltese DPA found that a controller failed to react to an access request within one month as the GDPR foresees, and failed to provide the data subject with a copy of their personal data.

The Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision after a complainant made an access request in August 2022 and got no full answer. The HR company named only the source of the data and gave no reply on the legal basis, retention period and other Article 15(1) information, and it did not respond within one month or notify an extension. The chamber found breaches of Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 15(1), and linked the accountability principle under Article 5(2) to informing the data subject of the source. It ordered the company to comply with the access request within 30 days and to notify the DPA; no fine was imposed at this stage.

A former security guard complained that Securitas A/S had passed his job title, full name and personal identification number to the Danish intelligence services (PET and FE) for a security clearance, without his consent. The Danish Data Protection Agency held that consent was not a valid GDPR basis in an employment relationship. It found instead that the disclosure was lawful under the legitimate interests basis in Article 6(1)(f) GDPR, because the clearance was needed for the employer to check the employee could do the job. The complaint was therefore not upheld and no criticism was made.

Romania's data protection authority concluded an investigation into a broker company in November 2022. An Excel record holding clients' personal data, including ID numbers and bank details, was published online by the company's administrator, exposing the data of at least 509 people. The company was fined RON 49,418 (about EUR 10,000) for failing to ensure that persons acting under its authority process data only on its instructions (Art. 32(4) GDPR). It received warnings for not informing the data subjects of the breach (Art. 34 GDPR) and for storing non-essential cookies without consent (Art. 4(5) of Law 506/2004).

A complainant, who headed a ward at Landspítali, complained that the Directorate of Health had disclosed to an NGO, in a letter sent after the NGO's complaints about patient care on that ward, that he had been placed on indefinite leave and replaced. Persónuvernd held that the Directorate had a legal duty to supervise health services, so the disclosure rested on a legal obligation; that it was fair, proportionate and limited to a summary of the case file; and that the complainant had no separate notice right under Article 14. It found the processing compliant and rejected the complaint. The decision was later amended after the complainant asked for it to be reopened.

A complainant, a sole-trader's car owner, objected to a personalised number plate of his car being shown for minutes in a Belgian TV fiction episode about a drug gang, and asked for its removal, which the broadcaster refused on artistic-freedom grounds. The Litigation Chamber found that, in these specific circumstances, the plate was personal data because people around the complainant could identify him through it. It then dismissed the main infringements of the accountability, data protection by design, erasure and DPO provisions, dismissed the Article 12(1) finding without further action, and issued a warning on the transparency duty in Article 12(4). No fine was imposed.
